notes.meaning: Paul starts answering questions from a letter the Corinthian Christians sent him. Some believers in Corinth were asking whether it was best to avoid sex and marriage completely. Paul agrees that staying single is a good and honorable choice, but he makes clear that it is not a requirement for everyone.

Because sexual temptation was everywhere in their city, Paul encourages adults to enter into marriage. Each man should have his own wife, and each woman her own husband. Marriage provides a healthy, holy relationship where physical desires can be honored without sinning.

Husbands and wives have a duty to show regular physical affection and love to each other. When two people marry, they share authority over each other's bodies in an equal and loving partnership. Neither spouse should treat their own body as completely independent or withhold affection out of pride.

Spouses must not stop physical intimacy unless both agree to take a short break to focus on prayer. After that special time of prayer is over, they need to come back together. If they stay apart too long, Satan can tempt them when their self-control grows weak.

Paul explains that this temporary pause for prayer is an allowance, not an order from God. He is not commanding married couples to separate for special devotions. He is simply permitting it for those who choose to do so by mutual agreement.

Paul mentions that he personally enjoys the freedom of being single and wishes others could experience it too. However, he knows that God gives different gifts to different people. One person receives the gift of living self-controlled while single, while another receives the gift of marriage.

Paul speaks to people who are currently unmarried and to widows. He advises that it is good for them to stay single, just like he is. Being single gives a person unique freedom to serve God without family worries.

If unmarried people find it too hard to control their sexual desires, Paul tells them they should get married. An honorable marriage is much better than burning with constant passion and falling into temptation. Marriage is God's good answer for those who do not have the gift of celibacy.

Paul gives an absolute rule for married believers that comes straight from Jesus' own teaching: a wife must not separate from her husband. If a separation does happen, she must stay unmarried or else seek peace and be reconciled with him, and a husband must not divorce his wife. Believers must treat marriage as a lifelong promise.

Paul turns to mixed marriages, where one spouse has become a Christian but the other has not. Jesus had not spoken directly on this situation during His earthly ministry, so Paul gives an inspired apostolic rule. If a Christian husband has an unbelieving wife who is willing to stay, he must not divorce her.

The same principle applies to a Christian woman with an unbelieving husband. If her husband is content to go on living with her, she should not divorce or leave him. Trusting in Christ does not cancel an existing marriage contract.

A believing spouse brings a holy influence into the entire household. The marriage is clean and acceptable in God's sight, and any children are set apart under God's blessing rather than being considered unclean. Believers can rest assured that staying in the marriage does not defile them.

differ.view: Children with even one believing parent belong to God's covenant people, his promise-family. This supports baptizing them as infants.
The verse says nothing about baptism. "Holy" means the children were born in a proper, God-approved marriage.
A child of a believer can be regarded as saved until the child is old enough to answer to God for themselves.

notes.meaning: If the unbelieving partner refuses to stay and walks away from the marriage, the believer should let them go. The Christian husband or wife is not trapped in bondage under those circumstances. God calls His people to live in peace rather than endless conflict.

differ.view: A believer deserted by an unbelieving spouse is freed from the marriage and may marry again.
The deserted believer may live apart in peace, but is not free to marry someone else.

notes.meaning: Paul reminds believers that their patient, faithful lives might lead their unbelieving spouses to trust in Christ. No one can guarantee that a partner will be saved, but God often works through a loving Christian in the home. A believer's quiet faithfulness gives strong hope for the family.

Paul lays down a general rule that applies to every church: each person should live faithfully in whatever situation God placed them in when they were called. Coming to faith does not mean an individual must overturn their social position or station in life. Christians should honor God right where they are.

Paul uses circumcision, the ancient Jewish covenant sign, to make his point. A Jewish believer should not try to erase the signs of his background, nor should a Gentile believer feel pressured to become circumcised. Faith in Jesus welcomes people from every background without requiring physical alterations.

Paul explains that outward ceremonies like circumcision have no spiritual power to save anyone. What matters completely to God is genuine obedience to His commandments flowing from faith. Outward rituals cannot take the place of a heart devoted to the Lord.

Paul repeats that every believer should remain content in the social rank or honest work they held when God saved them. Christian faith brings an inward change of heart rather than a need to quit a lawful station. A person can live a holy life in any honest occupation.

Paul addresses slaves who became Christians, telling them not to be weighed down with anxiety over their social condition. At the same time, if an opportunity comes to gain freedom lawfully, they should gladly take it. Earthly servitude does not stop a believer from fully serving Jesus Christ.

A slave who is called by the Lord receives spiritual freedom from sin and becomes Christ's freedman. In the same way, a free person who comes to faith becomes a willing slave of Christ. Every believer shares the same spiritual worth and answers to the same Master.

Christ paid a tremendous price by giving His life to purchase every believer. Because Christians belong solely to Him, they must not let themselves become spiritual slaves to human customs or ungodly leaders. Our primary loyalty must always be given to Jesus.

Paul repeats his key principle with warmth, urging everyone to walk closely with God in whatever situation they were called. No matter where a person stands in human society, God is present with them. True peace comes from remaining near to God every day.

Paul begins answering questions about young unmarried people, stating that Jesus gave no direct command about staying single. Instead, Paul offers his judgment as an apostle who has received mercy from God to be trustworthy. His guidance is given as wise advice rather than an ironclad law.

Because of the current hardships and persecution pressing on believers, Paul thinks it is best for people to stay as they are. In troubled times, having a family brings extra distress and worry. Staying single helps Christians endure trials with fewer earthly burdens.

Paul tells married men not to seek a separation from their wives. If a man is single or unmarried, he should not feel pressured to hurry out and look for a wife. Contentment in one's present condition helps a believer stay calm during troubled seasons.

Paul makes it clear that choosing to marry is not a sin for any single person. However, those who marry will experience extra trouble and pressure in this fallen world. Paul's gentle counsel is meant to spare believers from unnecessary hardship.

Paul reminds the church that earthly time is running short before the Lord returns. Because eternity is approaching, believers should hold earthly relationships with a loose grip rather than making them their absolute center. Christians must keep their eyes fixed on what lasts forever.

Believers should maintain balance in their sorrows, joys, and possessions. Christians should not be paralyzed by grief, carried away by temporary happiness, or attached to things they buy. Everything in this life is temporary and must be handled with eternity in view.

Christians are free to make lawful use of the things in this world, but they should never be consumed or ruled by them. The current outward form and system of this world is rapidly passing away. Believers should place their deepest hope in God's unchanging kingdom.

Paul wants believers to be free from distracting worries. An unmarried man can focus his thoughts entirely on the Lord's work and how to please Him. A married man must naturally spend time and energy caring for family needs and pleasing his wife, so his attention is divided.

The same difference is true for women. An unmarried woman or virgin can direct her full energy toward serving the Lord and staying holy in body and spirit. A married woman must look after household duties and care for her husband's welfare.

Paul explains that his counsel is designed to help the Corinthians, not to put a tight leash on their freedom. He wants to help them live in a fitting way with undivided devotion to God. His goal is to promote their spiritual well-being without making rules God did not make.

If someone responsible for a young woman feels he is acting unfairly toward her, and it seems right for her to marry, he should let the marriage take place. Giving permission to marry is not a sin. Marriage is a good and proper step when personal desires and circumstances call for it.

If a person has a settled conviction in his heart, feels no outside pressure, and decides to keep the young woman unmarried, he does well. Choosing singleness is a fine choice when it comes from clear resolve and peaceful agreement. Doing right requires standing firm without feeling forced.

Paul summarizes that giving someone in marriage is a good thing to do, because marriage is honorable. At the same time, deciding not to marry does even better under current hardships, because it spares a person earthly trouble and leaves them free to serve God. Both paths are honorable before the Lord.

A married woman is bound to her husband as long as he lives, and only his death sets her free from the marriage covenant. If her husband dies, she is completely free to remarry anyone she chooses, as long as he belongs to the Lord. A Christian widow should marry only a fellow believer.

Paul gives his judgment that a widow will generally find more peace and fewer troubles if she stays single. He states that he offers this advice under the guidance of God's Holy Spirit. His counsel helps believers choose what leads to lasting peace and focus on Christ.
